You hold Q, the middle card, and are in the final round. Your opponent checked, so you can either check (letting the pot go to you without risk) or bet (potentially extracting value if they fold, or forcing a call with a weaker hand). 

Opponent has a net score of -5, meaning they’ve lost 5 chips. They’ve folded in rounds 1, 7, and 6 (when you had K and Q), and called in rounds 3, 4, 5, 8. Their betting pattern suggests they bet with K and Q, but fold with J. In round 9, they checked—this is likely because they have J (the weakest card) and are trying to avoid losing more. 

You have Q, which beats J but loses to K. Since they checked, they likely have J. Betting now would be optimal: it risks nothing if they fold (which they likely will), and if they call (unlikely, since they’d have to have K, which they haven’t shown), you’d lose. But given their pattern, they probably have J and will fold. 

Betting maximizes expected value: you win 1 chip with a high probability (they fold), and only risk 1 chip if they call (which is unlikely). 

Thus, the best move is to bet.
